extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and researchers of film history, censorship, and religious/media studies
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and explaining the National Legion of Decency's standards and procedures for rating motion pictures (its pledge, rating categories, targeted content, and review process) as described in the Wikipedia article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pledge / directive to avoid films that 'offend decency and Christian morality'
rubrics_metrics.description: Members were asked to pledge to patronize only those motion pictures which did not "offend decency and Christian morality". The organization circulated a pledge asking Catholics to "remain away from all motion pictures except those which do not offend decency and Christian morality."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pledge text (1934 revision) included condemnation of indecent and immoral motion pictures and those which glorify crime or criminals; pledged to strengthen public opinion against such films and to stay away from places showing them. The pledge was administered in parishes (often annually) and used to mobilize Catholic avoidance of condemned films; it functioned as both moral guidance and a consumer boycott instrument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legion rating — A: Morally unobjectionable (with A-I, A-II subdivisions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Original rating 'A' = Morally unobjectionable. 'A' was subsequently split into A-I (for general patronage) and A-II (for adults and adolescents only) to distinguish films suitable for children from those more appropriate for older viewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to indicate films acceptable for Catholics; A-I = suitable for all audiences, A-II = suitable for adults and adolescents. The subdivision clarified age-appropriateness rather than content acceptability. Later further adult categories were added (see separate entry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Legion rating — A-III and A-IV (added adult categories)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two additional 'A' categories were later added: A-III for adults only, and A-IV for adults with reservations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Added in 1957 when the Legion increased its ratings panel expertise. A-IV in particular was controversial (examples include The Exorcist and Saturday Night Fever); its description was altered in 1995 to films "which are not morally offensive in themselves but are not for casual viewing." These categories marked content judged suitable only for mature audiences or requiring caution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legion rating — B: Morally objectionable in part
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicated films with some elements judged objectionable; historically films rated B might still be viewed by some Catholics with caution. In 1982 the B and C ratings were combined into a new 'O' rating (see separate entry). Studios sometimes removed or altered content to move a film from B to a less severe rating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legion rating — C: Condemned
rubrics_metrics.description: 'C' = Condemned (morally unacceptable). Practicing Catholics were directed to refrain from viewing such films.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'C' rating instructed Catholics to "remain away from all motion pictures except those which do not offend decency and Christian morality." Most C ratings tended to be applied to foreign films; condemnation could harm a film's distribution because many Catholics pledged to avoid condemned films. The C rating existed from 1933 until the end of 1981.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legion/NCOMP rating — O: 'morally offensive' (replacement for B and C)
rubrics_metrics.description: On January 1, 1982 the B and C ratings were combined into a new 'O' rating for "morally offensive" films.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCOMP began to reassign ratings of some older films based on the new system. 'O' consolidated previously separate partially objectionable and condemned categories into a single designation of moral offensiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of content targeted by the Legion and earlier codes
rubrics_metrics.description: The Legion and earlier censorship/self-regulation efforts targeted content such as nudity, illicit sexual relationships, suicide, drug abuse, promiscuous sex, venereal disease, polygamy, child marriages, prostitution, and films that "glorify crime or criminals." Exploitation films dealing with lurid/taboo subjects were singled out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited: the 1933 film Ecstasy (nudity, illicit affair, suicide) was condemned; The Pace That Kills (cocaine addiction, amorality, prostitution) was condemned. Studios sometimes removed dialogue or made revisions (e.g., This Thing Called Love had fifteen lines removed) to avoid harsher ratings. The Legion was often more conservative than the industry's Production Code.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production Code / Hays Code ('The Formula' and 'Don'ts and Be Carefuls')
rubrics_metrics.description: The Production Code (Hays Code) was an industry-authored set of rules—begun with 'The Formula' and the later 'Don'ts and Be Carefuls'—outlining issues and subjects movies should avoid as a means of self-regulation and to forestall government censorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Formula requested studios send synopses to the MPPDA for review; the 'Don'ts and Be Carefuls' listed topics filmmakers were advised to avoid or handle cautiously. Enforcement was initially weak (SRC overwhelmed), and studios frequently ignored recommendations until later enforcement via the Production Code Administration. The Production Code influenced the kinds of content the Legion and others targeted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thirteen Points (NAMPI) — list of subjects/storylines to avoid
rubrics_metrics.description: The National Association of the Motion Picture Industry (NAMPI) devised a list known as the 'Thirteen Points'—subjects and storylines the industry promised to avoid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Thirteen Points were an early industry-content restriction intended to head off censorship, but there was no enforcement mechanism and NAMPI proved ineffective in preventing problematic material; nevertheless some items later became part of the Production Code.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rating review process and procedures used by the Legion/NCOMP
rubrics_metrics.description: By the late 1950s films judged 'problematic' were viewed two or three times: first by staff and then by consultants who provided written evaluations. The Legion increased the membership of its ratings panel to include individuals knowledgeable in film and communication arts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The process included multiple screenings, written consultant evaluations, and panel deliberation. This procedural guidance indicates a structured review intended to balance moral judgment with film expertise; nonetheless the Legion's judgments were nonbinding and sometimes viewed as either too liberal or too cautious.

rubrics_metrics.name: United States Conference of Catholic Bishops (USCCB) Office for Film and Broadcasting continuation of rating practice
rubrics_metrics.description: The USCCB Office for Film and Broadcasting continued the National Legion of Decency's rating system (A: with A-I/A-II/A-III; B; C) and reviewed motion pictures, radio, and television using the same scale and goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office aimed to 'rid the screen of stories that lowered traditional moral standards' and reviewed every movie in the United States for decades. It maintained the same basic definitions (A = unobjectionable with subcategories; B = objectionable in part; C = condemned) until later organizational changes and eventual shutdowns; archived reviews were maintained by Catholic News Service and successors.
